hero.headline: Fort Pierce Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit invites visitors to explore Florida coastal habitats
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce offers rare close-up encounters with marine life, displaying fully live models of ecosystems dating back to 1980.
hero.body:
Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce houses more species than many larger exhibits. The philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. Hoffman told WPTV that they feel like they are the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast and they do not want to be.

The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms. The exhibit's touch tank is another crowd favorite, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff guidance.

Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. The facility is open to the public year-round.

cards.headline: Increased homestead exemption could cost Florida local governments $11.86 billion annually, state economists warn
cards.teaser: State economists released figures Friday showing that a constitutional amendment to increase homestead exemptions could eventually extract $11.86 billion per ye.
cards.body:
State economists released figures Friday showing that a constitutional amendment to increase homestead exemptions could eventually extract $11.86 billion per year from the budgets of Florida's 67 counties. The Revenue Estimating Conference analysis comes more than a week after lawmakers passed HJR 1-F, which will appear on the November ballot and would raise homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with further increases tied to the Consumer Price Index. The fiscal impact would escalate over time, according to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research. Local governments could see nearly $5 billion less revenue in FY 27-28, increasing to $8.775 billion in FY 28-29, $9.7 billion in FY 29-30, and $10.751 billion in FY 30-31.

Commuter counties with lower commercial development face the steepest proportional losses. St. Lucie could lose 35% of revenue, while Clay, Baker, Citrus, and Hernando Counties could all face losses exceeding 30%. Flagler County, Volusia County, Hernando County, and Sumter County would all see at least two-thirds of homes potentially impacted. Larger urban counties face the biggest raw dollar losses, with Miami-Dade facing a $445 million revenue decrease by FY 28-29, Hillsborough losing $353 million, Broward down roughly $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce teen shooting sparks community safety concerns
cards.teaser: The critical shooting of a Fort Pierce teenager has raised concerns among local residents about youth safety in the community.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce teenager remains in critical condition following a shooting that has heightened community concerns about youth violence. Three juveniles have been arrested in connection with the incident, which occurred recently in Fort Pierce.

Local residents have expressed alarm about the shooting. "It's terrifying because it could be your child," one community member said, reflecting fears about youth safety in Fort Pierce neighborhoods.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds vows to use constitutional commission for property tax cuts if November amendment fails
cards.teaser: The leading Republican candidate for Governor says he will revive homestead exemption increases through the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission if voters reject the measure in November.
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds said Friday on Fox Business that if HJR 1-F fails to reach the 60% threshold in November, he will use Florida's constitutional Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to pursue property tax relief. The Naples Republican, who qualified for the gubernatorial race this week with President Donald Trump's endorsement, told viewers the commission would study all taxes and fees with the goal of eliminating homestead property taxes or providing real relief to seniors on fixed income and working families. The TBRC is scheduled to convene next January for the first time in two decades, soon after the next governor is sworn in, and could advance an amendment for the 2028 ballot.

HJR 1-F would raise the homestead exemption on non-school levies to $150,000 next year and $250,000 in 2028. Donalds defended Governor Ron DeSantis against criticism from the Wall Street Journal editorial board, which criticized the plan as poorly designed. He said property taxes in Florida have doubled over the last decade while seniors and working families struggle to make ends meet. The voters of Florida will decide this November, Donalds said, noting that the Legislature proposes measures for the ballot but cannot make changes themselves.

cards.headline: 28-year-old West Palm Beach man killed in motorcycle crash at Boynton Beach intersection
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia died Friday morning after his 2007 Kawasaki Ninja struck a Kia Forte at Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road.
cards.body:
Albert Garcia was riding eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed around 7:08 a.m. Friday when he approached the intersection with El Clair Ranch Road. A 39-year-old Boynton Beach man driving a 2016 Kia Forte was stopped in the westbound lanes attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road.

As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point.

Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as first from St. Lucie County named Southeast Youth of the Year
cards.body:
For the first time in its history, Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County has produced a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of Port St. Lucie High School, earned the prestigious award and will compete for the national title at the Youth of the Year competition in New York City on October 1. The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award recognizes standout teens who demonstrate dedication to academics, strong values, and leadership in service.

Enrique's path reflects remarkable resilience. He arrived in Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without speaking English. With support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he transformed into a confident leader and scholar. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." As Florida Youth of the Year and his high school's valedictorian, Enrique will attend the University of Florida this fall. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, praised his ability to turn challenges into opportunities while maintaining humility. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and longtime Youth of the Year judge, said Enrique impressed judges from the beginning and is ready for national competition.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach Boulevard crash
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach resident died Friday morning after his motorcycle collided with a car at a major intersection in Boynton Beach. The crash occurred around 7:08 a.m. at Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Albert Garcia was operating a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja when the fatal accident happened.

Investigators determined that Garcia was traveling eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high speed as he neared the intersection. At the same moment, a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was operating a 2016 Kia Forte in the westbound lanes. The Kia driver had stopped and was attempting to turn left onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road when the collision occurred.

As the Kia began its left turn, Garcia braked his motorcycle but could not stop in time to avoid impact. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia in the intersection. The force of the collision threw Garcia from the bike, and he landed southwest of the crash site. Emergency rescue crews transported him to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. According to investigators, Garcia was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident.

The driver of the Kia was properly restrained with a seatbelt and escaped injury from the crash. No other details about potential citations or ongoing investigations were provided by the sheriff's office. The incident marks another serious traffic fatality at a major Boynton Beach intersection.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reenters District 6 Commission race after Trump endorsement
cards.teaser: Sara Baxter reversed her decision to run for Congress and returned to the District 6 race by the noon qualifying deadline Saturday with President Donald Trump's endorsement.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race after reversing her decision to run for Congress, meeting the noon qualifying deadline with President Donald Trump's endorsement. Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomondo and Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker criticized the move, saying voters need someone committed to the district's issues rather than focused on a White House endorsement. "It doesn't make sense to me," Accomondo said. Tinker said Baxter "lost a lot of ground and a lot of credibility as a Republican candidate." Both emphasized community needs should be the priority. Baxter responded to the criticism in a statement: "This election is about people, NOT politics."

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman outlined their platforms in statements. Waldron said she entered the race because District 6 needs focused leadership on traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth. Guzman said residents deserve a candidate committed to public needs who will bring stability and minimize negativity. The main issues facing District 6 are development, traffic, and the emergence of AI data centers. The primary election is Aug. 18, with the general election in November.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reverses decision, reenters District 6 Commission race after Trump endorsement
hero.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter dropped her congressional bid and reentered the race for the District 6 Commission seat after President Donald Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter is running for the District 6 Commission seat after reversing her earlier decision to run for Congress. She met the noon qualifying deadline to enter the race and received an endorsement from President Donald Trump, who reportedly asked her to stay in Palm Beach County rather than pursue a congressional seat.

The other candidates in the race have questioned Baxter's sudden reversal and argued that voters should prioritize commitment to the district over presidential endorsements. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomondo expressed skepticism about the decision, while Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker said he believes Baxter has damaged her credibility as a Republican candidate. Both emphasized that the focus should remain on addressing community needs rather than national political connections. "What's important is that we take care of the true needs of the community first, first and foremost," Accomondo said. Tinker added that his focus is on the people, stating "if it's not about the people, I'm out."

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman released statements outlining their priorities for the district. Waldron emphasized that District 6 needs focused leadership on traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth. Guzman called for a candidate committed to serving the public and bringing stability to the district. According to reporting from WPTV, the main issues facing District 6 include development, traffic, and the emergence of AI data centers.

Baxter responded to the criticism from her opponents by emphasizing that the election should focus on constituents rather than political considerations. "This election is about people, NOT politics," she said. The primary election for District 6 is scheduled for August 18, with the general election to follow in November. Voters will ultimately decide which candidate best represents their interests and priorities in the race.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses thrift stores to house cats during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast shifted many of its cats to two thrift store locations while its adoption, customer service, and intake areas undergo construction in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to house adoptable cats during a major renovation of its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily relocating many cats to store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside merchandise at both thrift stores. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted. The organization is also seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Hundreds of fish die in Port St. Lucie after city algae treatment at Sawgrass Lakes
cards.teaser: Dead fish floated in the water at the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday after the city hired a vendor to treat the water for algae earlier in the week.
cards.body:
Dead fish floated across Sawgrass Lakes in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning after the city treated the water for algae on Tuesday and Wednesday. The city hired vendor SOLitude to conduct the treatment. Neighbor Jim Herbert reported hundreds and hundreds of fish died, with thousands of small fish gulping air. Experts told WPTV that high heat combined with algae treatment can make water uninhabitable for aquatic life. Crews removed the dead fish Thursday and tested oxygen levels in the water. Herbert said this was at least the second fish die-off since he lived in the neighborhood.

Scott Samples with the city of Port St. Lucie said officials have been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions. "We're hoping that there might be a couple of options soon," Samples said, noting those options depend on several factors. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, said the city should consider more natural solutions, including planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that fuels algae growth. "We're going to end up in a cycle that we can't break unless we go back to square one and start with a natural remediation," Moir said.

cards.headline: Wrongful death lawsuit filed in St. Lucie County Florida Turnpike crash that killed three
cards.teaser: The daughter of a woman killed in an August 2025 Florida Turnpike crash in St. Lucie County has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the truck driver, his employer White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were killed in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. Joseph's 22-year-old daughter, Angeline Dowdian, filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. The lawsuit is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer.

Bello argues that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. The case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warned the company may reopen under another name.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce displays live coastal habitats
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats with fully live models of ecosystems dating back to 1980.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through fully live, complex ecosystem models. Manager Bill Hoffman said the facility's philosophy of displaying these intricate habitats dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran. The facility operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Indian River County warns property tax amendment could cost $50 million in 2028
cards.teaser: Indian River County leaders told residents Friday the property tax amendment on the November ballot could eliminate $50 million from the county's $597 million b.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to warn residents about a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The proposed measure would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss said the state would dictate to local governments how they fund services, noting that every county is different and funds what the community wants. County officials predicted the amendment could eliminate $50 million from the county's $597 million budget by 2028, representing a substantial loss for Indian River County even if comparable to larger counties like Orlando or Miami.

Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called the measure an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy and described it as a tax shift rather than a tax cut. He warned the county would likely need to raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to offset lost revenue. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of the department's funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Brewer noted that three projected fire stations may not be built if the amendment passes. Moss accused Tallahassee of declaring war on local government.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis announces Medicaid fraud prevention measures in West Palm Beach targeting Southeast Florida operations
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced new Medicaid fraud prevention measures Friday at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County, targeting what officials described as sophisticated criminal operations concentrated in Southeast Florida.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced sweeping Medicaid fraud prevention measures during a press conference Friday afternoon in West Palm Beach at the Health Care District of Palm Beach County. DeSantis identified Southeast Florida as a fraud hotspot, noting that while Palm Beach County is affected, Miami-Dade and Broward counties face even greater challenges. Agency for Healthcare Administration Secretary Shevaun L. Harris revealed that more than a dozen entities presenting themselves as Medicaid providers in West Palm Beach were actually staged operations created solely to steal from the state program. Investigators discovered the fake operations through shared addresses across multiple unrelated entities, suspicious ownership structures, and no evidence of actual patient care. Harris stated the state is pursuing those responsible, saying "We're coming for you. We have more tools, more investigators, and more resolve than ever."

The state announced three major initiatives to combat fraud. First, AHCA is launching a pilot program with Ventolin, an identity fraud detection company that will identify stolen IDs, synthetic IDs, and hidden ownership structures. Second, AHCA imposed enrollment moratoriums on high-risk provider categories including durable medical equipment suppliers and adult day care providers. Third, the state is requiring all active Florida Medicaid providers to revalidate credentials and identity. Harris said Florida's program integrity efforts have saved $136.45 million in recovery and prevention benefits, with AHCA terminating or denying enrollment to more than 3,200 providers over the past two years.

cards.headline: Lake Worth woman born without right hand goes viral after Palm Beach County deputy's traffic stop accusation
cards.teaser: Katie Thomas was pulled over by a Palm Beach County deputy who accused her of holding her phone in her right hand while driving, but Thomas was born without a right hand. The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth resident Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving, unaware that Thomas was born without a right hand. Body camera footage shows the deputy telling Thomas, "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone. I mean, I saw you." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. When the deputy pressed further, Thomas replied, "Hand to God, you did not have your phone in your hand." The traffic stop has generated 110 million views on social media. The citation was dropped for lack of evidence.

Thomas, an adaptive athlete who has spent her life raising awareness for the limb-difference community, told WPTV that being accused of something she did not have a limb to be accused of was "probably one of the most captivating things about the whole thing" because it was "immediately apparent to 110 million people, that what he claims he saw was impossible." The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review is underway. Thomas harbors no ill will and would welcome a conversation about using the moment to raise awareness about limb differences. She has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. Thomas said she has no plans to sue.

cards.headline: Curaçao soccer fans from Port St. Lucie travel to Boca Raton to witness World Cup training ahead of historic debut
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday with jerseys and flags in hand to witness Curaçao's preparation for its historic first-ever World Cup appearance. The "Blue Wave" held a training session that drew enthusiastic supporters eager to see their favorite players ahead of the team's debut match against Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas. Curaçao, an island nation with a population of just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches.

Goalkeeper Eloy Room told WPTV the outpouring of support has fueled the team's excitement. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today. It gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said. He added, "We fought long for this moment to play in the World Cup. Now we're here, we're going to show the world what we can and the first game is going to be a nice one." Midfielder Tahitch Chong reflected on the moment's significance for the island. "I think it's amazing to see. I don't think the people back home are going to believe the crowd we had here," Chong said. Fans traveled from across South Florida, including Marionella Barzeycoggins from Port St. Lucie, who brought her entire family to the event.

hero.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores house adoptable cats during Palm City shelter renovation
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
hero.body:
The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find not only unique items for sale but also adoptable cats at both thrift stores. The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues.

Ellis noted that donations of gently used goods are welcome. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman explained that the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, distinguishing it from most public aquariums. Hoffman told WPTV the aquarium houses more species than many larger exhibits, including a barracuda measuring just four inches. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms.

The touch tank serves as another crowd favorite, where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. Operating in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit aims to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced by live displays. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library launches free summer STREAM programs for kids and teens
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library offers kids and teens free STREAM summer programs, lunches, and family nights in downtown Delray Beach.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM programs throughout the summer for children and teenagers at its downtown location on Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue. According to Kae Jonsons, director of development and community relations, the library has served the community since 1913, when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection. The facility now welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually to its 36,000-square-foot space.

Natalie Baron, young adult librarian, is leading sessions like ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also join lab-based activities including collaborative 3D puzzle builds and pick up themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, encouraging young readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and take home an Unearth a Story bag with a free STREAM book and activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to youth up to 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children ages 5 and older to explore STREAM topics together. Saturday Science Discovery programs for ages 9 to 12 feature hands-on archaeology activities including Piece Together History, trash bag archaeology, carbon dating, and fossil hunts. Upcoming Thursday speakers include Malachi Fenn from the Florida Public Archaeology Network on June 11, Sea Turtle Adventures beach cleanup on June 25, American Shark Conservancy's SharkSmarts on July 2, and FPAN Beyond Artifacts on July 16. For a complete program schedule and registration information, visitors can visit delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: DeSantis publicly rebukes Florida GOP Chair Evan Power over debate criteria for gubernatorial candidates
hero.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis criticized the Republican Party of Florida for using what he called ridiculous criteria to avoid holding debates between gubernatorial candidates.
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has openly challenged Florida GOP Chair Evan Power's decision to prevent direct debates between gubernatorial candidates at the party's upcoming Sunshine Showdown event. The conflict centers on the Republican Party of Florida's debate eligibility requirements, which mandate that candidates achieve 10 percent support in the party's internal polling, raise more than $10 million, and secure donations from more than 10,000 contributors. Power announced on X that candidates would be permitted to speak at the event but would not be allowed to directly engage each other in debates.

DeSantis responded directly to Power's announcement with a sharp public criticism. He argued that Power should not insult the intelligence of Republican voters by using what he called ridiculous criteria to break a debate promise and manipulate the outcome in favor of a preferred candidate. DeSantis questioned why the party would not simply allocate 90 minutes, secure a television partner, and allow candidates to debate each other directly. He suggested that the only logical explanation for refusing such debates would be if party leadership prioritized outside interests over the welfare of voters. During a Friday press conference, DeSantis elaborated on his position, stating that the party should play only a limited role in the gubernatorial race. He emphasized that the process should be driven by candidates themselves rather than decided by unelected party officials. He encouraged candidates to arrange debates through television, radio, and other available formats.

Other Republican figures have echoed DeSantis's criticism. Jay Collins retweeted the governor's statement and reinforced his argument against insulting voter intelligence. While Collins acknowledged that debates alone would not determine the race's outcome, he called on voters to notice if Byron Donalds declines to participate in debates and instead remains sheltered by the Republican Party of Florida. James Fishback also expressed agreement with DeSantis's position. Former House Speaker Paul Renner questioned whether the Florida GOP had become indistinguishable from the Democratic Party in light of the debate restrictions.

The dispute reflects ongoing tension between DeSantis and Congressman Donalds. DeSantis has repeatedly criticized Donalds over recent months, contending that the Trump-aligned congressman provided no support for battles DeSantis led in recent years. Despite the governor's public criticism and the debate controversy surrounding his candidacy, Donalds has stated he remains unconcerned about the situation. The conflict underscores how the gubernatorial race on the Republican side, despite being heavily favored to one candidate, continues to generate internal party friction.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds vows to use constitutional commission for property tax cuts if November amendment fails
cards.teaser: The leading Republican candidate for Governor says he will revive homestead exemption increases through the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission if voters reject the measure in November.
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds said Friday on Fox Business that if HJR 1-F fails to reach the 60% threshold in November, he will use Florida's constitutional Taxation and Budget Reform Commission to pursue property tax relief. The Naples Republican, who qualified for the gubernatorial race this week with President Donald Trump's endorsement, told viewers the commission would study all taxes and fees with the goal of eliminating homestead property taxes or providing real relief to seniors on fixed income and working families. The TBRC is scheduled to convene next January for the first time in two decades, soon after the next governor is sworn in, and could advance an amendment for the 2028 ballot.

HJR 1-F would raise the homestead exemption on non-school levies to $150,000 next year and $250,000 in 2028. Donalds defended Governor Ron DeSantis against criticism from the Wall Street Journal editorial board, which criticized the plan as poorly designed. He said property taxes in Florida have doubled over the last decade while seniors and working families struggle to make ends meet. The voters of Florida will decide this November, Donalds said, noting that the Legislature proposes measures for the ballot but cannot make changes themselves.

cards.headline: Increased homestead exemption could cost Florida local governments $11.86 billion annually, state economists warn
cards.teaser: State economists released figures Friday showing that a constitutional amendment to increase homestead exemptions could eventually extract $11.86 billion per ye.
cards.body:
State economists released figures Friday showing that a constitutional amendment to increase homestead exemptions could eventually extract $11.86 billion per year from the budgets of Florida's 67 counties. The Revenue Estimating Conference analysis comes more than a week after lawmakers passed HJR 1-F, which will appear on the November ballot and would raise homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with further increases tied to the Consumer Price Index. The fiscal impact would escalate over time, according to the Office of Economic and Demographic Research. Local governments could see nearly $5 billion less revenue in FY 27-28, increasing to $8.775 billion in FY 28-29, $9.7 billion in FY 29-30, and $10.751 billion in FY 30-31.

Commuter counties with lower commercial development face the steepest proportional losses. St. Lucie could lose 35% of revenue, while Clay, Baker, Citrus, and Hernando Counties could all face losses exceeding 30%. Flagler County, Volusia County, Hernando County, and Sumter County would all see at least two-thirds of homes potentially impacted. Larger urban counties face the biggest raw dollar losses, with Miami-Dade facing a $445 million revenue decrease by FY 28-29, Hillsborough losing $353 million, Broward down roughly $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds introduces federal bill requiring states and cities to open books for audits as condition of funding
cards.teaser: The Tax Dollar Accountability Act would require state and local governments to grant the Comptroller of the Currency total access to records to show how federal money is used.
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds introduced the Tax Dollar Accountability Act this week, requiring subsidiary governments to show the Comptroller of the Currency how federal money is used by granting total access to records. Detailed budgets, expenditure reports, vendor contracts, and grant distributions would have to be presented after every fiscal year to show compliance with the terms of the appropriation. The bill was filed following widely-reported misappropriations of Medicaid and COVID-19 funding in various states. Donalds explained the bill during a Fox News appearance Saturday as a necessary corrective for $200 billion of misallocated payments identified already. He stated that if any local or state agency gets federal dollars, the documents around those federal dollars have to be made available to the federal government so they can be audited at any given time. "Local jurisdictions have a responsibility that if you're going to get taxpayer dollars, then your books need to be open and subject to audit by the federal government," Donalds said.

Governor Ron DeSantis announced Friday a Medicaid integrity initiative that will strengthen screening of providers, use technology to drill down on fraud, control enrollment for high-risk provider categories, and revalidate active Medicaid providers. Donalds vowed that if elected Governor, he will continue what DeSantis has begun. "We will DOGE all local governments and all state agencies. There will be no sacred cows because the taxpayers deserve to make sure that their dollars are being spent efficiently and transparently," the Naples Congressman said.

cards.headline: Attorney General James Uthmeier endorses Scott Singer in crowded Republican primary for Congressional District 25
cards.teaser: The statewide endorsement gives former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer another marquee name in a Republican primary field that includes five candidates.
cards.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier endorsed Scott Singer this week in Florida's Republican primary for Congressional District 25. Uthmeier wrote on X that Singer, the former Boca Raton Mayor, is a proven conservative who consistently fought to lower taxes, support small businesses, and stand strong behind law enforcement. Singer faces former state Rep. George Moraitis, Joe Kaufman, Daniel Franzese, and Raven Harrison in the August primary. Claudia Villatoro suspended her campaign this week.

Congressional District 25 was redrawn by Governor Ron DeSantis' office during a Special Session in late April and signed in May to favor the GOP. The seat stretches from Delray Beach in Palm Beach County through Broward and into Miami Beach in Miami-Dade County, territory President Donald Trump carried by 9 points in 2024. A Beacon Insights poll in early May found Singer trailing on his home turf while Moraitis ran closer to the likely Democratic nominee, Jared Moskowitz. Moskowitz, a two-term incumbent, launched his re-election bid rather than retire after redistricting reshaped his seat. Moskowitz faces Democratic Socialist Oliver Larkin in his own primary and closed the first quarter with roughly $1.2 million on hand. Uthmeier, endorsed by Trump for a full term, has also endorsed Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power in CD 2.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds unveils Read to Succeed plan to boost childhood literacy in Florida schools
cards.teaser: The gubernatorial candidate's plan includes science-of-reading teacher training, early intervention for K-2 students, and a new statewide award for teachers who excel in literacy instruction.
cards.body:
Byron Donalds revealed his Read to Succeed plan Saturday, a gubernatorial campaign initiative incorporating science-of-reading-based teacher training, early intervention for K-2 students, extra tutoring for Grade 3 students, and a new statewide Read to Succeed Award for teachers who excel in helping students overcome reading challenges. "When children learn to read by third grade, you've opened every door ahead of them. When they fall behind, those doors of opportunity are closed," Donalds said. The third-term Congressman added that Florida is choosing to open doors for every child, in every classroom, in every county.

Childhood literacy remains a significant challenge in Florida, which ranks worse than 44 other states in reading recovery, with 44% of 4th graders unable to read on grade level. Donalds will seek Title funding waivers from President Donald Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon to support literacy programs, including incentives for districts that demonstrate gains. Donalds characterized the plan as empowering parents and teachers with tools, technology, and tutoring rather than imposing a new mandate. Throughout his campaign, he has prioritized childhood education, advocating for individual learning plans for all students and long-term Student Success Plans beginning no later than sixth grade to help young people pursue career pathways.

cards.headline: St. Johns County Commission races finalized as growth debate dominates upcoming election
cards.teaser: Qualifying closed Friday for key county commission seats in one of Florida's fastest-growing counties, where development remains the central campaign issue two years after slow-growth candidates unseated incumbents.
cards.body:
Candidate qualifying closed at noon Friday, finalizing the ballot for key St. Johns County races that will test voter sentiment on growth and development in one of Florida's fastest-growing counties. Two years ago, candidates running on slow-the-growth platforms unseated incumbent County Commissioners they viewed as too favorable to developers. A third candidate with a similar message narrowly lost to incumbent Christian Whitehurst. Growth and development remain central issues in the 2026 election.

Commissioner Sarah Arnold is not seeking re-election in District 2, leaving an open seat with four Republicans. Former FBI agent Martin Pyszczymuka is running under the slogan "Slow the growth, stop the waste." Consultant Wilson McMullan emphasizes balancing economic development with preservation, advocating smarter planning and supporting manufacturing and aerospace job growth. St. Johns County Sheriff's Capt. Tim Burres, endorsed by the Fraternal Order of Police, cites overdevelopment as a primary campaign issue. Citibank executive Heather Brofford entered the race shortly before the qualifying deadline, prioritizing transportation, public safety, emergency services, and infrastructure to support population growth. As of the end of May, Pyszczymuka leads fundraising with nearly $28,000, closely followed by McMullan with roughly $27,000. In District 4, first-term Commissioner Krista Joseph faces two Republican challengers. Joseph was elected in 2022 after defeating incumbent Commissioner Jeremiah Blocker in the Republican primary despite being significantly outspent. Fellow Commissioners formally censured her in December 2023 after she urged voters to remove her colleagues from office. She lost her board chair position in late 2025 and has publicly clashed with Commissioner Clay Murphy, a slow-growth candidate elected in 2024. Retired law enforcement officer Sam Williams leads fundraising with more than $56,000, more than double Joseph's total. Attorney James Galloway also qualified, citing congestion and rapid growth as the county's most pressing concerns. Both races will be decided in the August primary.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter returns to District 6 race after reversing Congress decision
hero.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race after President Donald Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County.
hero.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter has rejoined the race for the District 6 Commission seat after deciding against a run for Congress. She met the noon qualifying deadline and secured an endorsement from President Donald Trump, who reportedly asked her to remain focused on Palm Beach County.

Her decision to stay in the local race has drawn criticism from other candidates who argue that voters should prioritize the district's specific needs over national political endorsements. Republican Elizabeth Accomondo and Democrat Rudolph Tinker both said the focus should remain on community issues rather than the White House endorsement. Tinker stated that Baxter has "lost a lot of ground and a lot of credibility as a Republican candidate," while Accomondo emphasized that taking care of the community's true needs should come first. Tinker added, "For me, it's about the people, and if it's not about the people, I'm out."

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman released similar statements expressing their commitment to district-focused leadership. Waldron said she entered the race because "District 6 needs focused leadership on issues like traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth." Guzman stressed that "the residents of District 6 deserve a candidate who is committed to the needs of our public" and emphasized the importance of bringing stability to the district. According to conversations with voters and candidates, the primary concerns facing District 6 include development, traffic congestion, and the emergence of AI data centers as a new issue for the community.

Baxter responded to her opponents' criticism in a statement, saying "This election is about people, NOT politics." The primary election is scheduled for August 18, with the general election to follow in November. Voters will ultimately decide which candidate best represents their interests in the District 6 race.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
cards.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, a Port St.
cards.body:
For the first time in its history, Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County has produced a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian at Port St. Lucie High School, earned the honor and will compete for the national title at the National Youth of the Year competition in New York City on Oct. 1. The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award recognizes standout teens across Boys & Girls Clubs who demonstrate dedication to academics, strong values, and leadership in service.

Enrique's path to this achievement began eight years ago when he arrived from the Dominican Republic without speaking English. Through encouragement from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he worked to grow and thrive, eventually becoming his high school's valedictorian and Florida Youth of the Year. This fall, he will attend the University of Florida. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, noted that Enrique has turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others with humility and determination. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and longtime Youth of the Year judge, said Enrique stood out from the start and is ready for the national competition. Enrique's parents expressed gratitude to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping their son grow as a leader and person.

cards.headline: Ian Andrew O'Connor dies in Stuart
cards.teaser: Ian Andrew O'Connor of Stuart has died, according to Treasure Coast Seawinds Funeral Home & Crematory.
cards.body: Services are being handled by Treasure Coast Seawinds Funeral Home & Crematory in Stuart. The obituary was published Friday.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach motorcyclist killed in Boynton Beach crash
cards.teaser: Albert Garcia, 28, of West Palm Beach died Friday after his motorcycle collided with a car at Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed Friday morning in a crash at a busy Boynton Beach intersection, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. The crash happened around 7:08 a.m. at the intersection of Boynton Beach Boulevard and El Clair Ranch Road. Investigators said Albert Garcia was riding a 2007 Kawasaki Ninja eastbound on Boynton Beach Boulevard at a high rate of speed as he approached the intersection.

At the same time, a 2016 Kia Forte driven by a 39-year-old Boynton Beach man was stopped in the westbound lanes of Boynton Beach Boulevard and attempting to make a left turn onto southbound El Clair Ranch Road. As the Kia began turning left, Garcia applied the motorcycle's brakes but did not have enough time or distance to avoid a collision. The motorcycle struck the passenger side of the Kia inside the intersection. Garcia was thrown from the motorcycle and landed a short distance southwest of the impact point. Rescue crews transported Garcia to Delray Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver of the Kia was wearing a seatbelt and was not injured. Garcia was wearing a helmet.

cards.headline: Delray Beach explores new memorial for Pulse victims amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: A committee has proposed a rainbow pyramid monument for Delray Beach to honor victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre, but Senate Bill 1134 poses legal barriers to the project.
cards.body:
Friday marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people died. In Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted Pride mural honoring the victims was sandblasted away in August 2025 by the Florida Department of Transportation to comply with statewide regulations removing political and ideological messaging from roadways. The mural had been created and funded by local residents and sat just blocks from downtown. The state also removed the rainbow crosswalk outside Pulse in Orlando, while Boynton Beach preemptively took theirs down and West Palm Beach removed a Pride crosswalk in Northwood before later replacing it with a rainbow corner in a nearby park.

The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee, formed by local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents, designed a proposal by March for a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color and illuminated at night. Dunayer believes Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the Pride mural once was, would be the perfect location. Commissioner Juli Casal said the delay stems from Senate Bill 1134, which awaits the governor's decision. The bill passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House and would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Casal stated that if private funding and private property were secured, the memorial could be completed quickly without needing city involvement.

cards.headline: Ed W Farrell dies in Jensen Beach
cards.teaser: Ed W Farrell of Jensen Beach has died, according to All County Funeral Home & Crematory.
cards.body: Services are being handled by All County Funeral Home & Crematory - Treasure Coast Chapel. Further details were published Saturday.

cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office has identified a rookie deputy who was seen tackling a suspect on a golf course.
cards.body: Details about the deputy's identity and the incident were published Friday. The incident occurred at a golf course in Martin County.

hero.headline: World Cup watch parties planned from Boca Raton to Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: Bars and venues from Boca Raton to Fort Pierce are hosting World Cup watch parties for soccer fans across the Treasure Coast.
hero.body:
World Cup watch parties are being organized at multiple venues stretching from Boca Raton to Fort Pierce, giving soccer fans opportunities to watch the tournament with fellow supporters. The events offer gathering places for fans across the region.

Fort Pierce is among the cities hosting watch parties for the international soccer tournament. The World Cup draws viewership from diverse communities across South Florida and the Treasure Coast.

cards.headline: Daughter of St. Lucie County crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit against trucking company, freight broker
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian, whose mother Faniola Joseph died in an Aug. 12, 2025 crash on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against truck driver Harjinder Singh, White Hawk Carriers and freight broker C.H. Robinson.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Singh worked for White Hawk Carriers, a company with a troubling safety record. Faniola Joseph had been living in Indiana and had come south to purchase goods to resell in her shop.

Joseph's only child, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. She is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down. Bello argues the crash was not an accident but "a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives."

cards.headline: Fort Pierce teen critically injured in shooting, three juveniles arrested
cards.teaser: A teenage boy was critically injured in a Fort Pierce shooting, and three juveniles have been arrested in connection with the incident.
cards.body:
The shooting left a teenage boy in critical condition in Fort Pierce. Three juveniles were arrested following the incident, though additional details about the circumstances of the shooting have not been disclosed.

The arrest of three juveniles indicates law enforcement has identified suspects in the case. The investigation continues as the injured teen remains in critical condition.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor charged with child neglect of five foster children
cards.teaser: A pastor in Fort Pierce has been charged with child neglect involving five foster children in his care.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges related to five foster children. The charges indicate alleged failures in the care and supervision of the children placed in the pastor's home.

The case involves multiple foster children, suggesting systemic issues in the care provided. Criminal charges of child neglect can carry significant penalties under Florida law.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County 2026 election candidates finalized after qualifying deadline
cards.teaser: The candidate slate for St. Lucie County's 2026 elections is now set following the close of the qualifying period.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County's 2026 election candidates are now official after the qualifying deadline passed. The finalized candidate list will determine the races voters will see on their ballots this year.

Qualifying is the formal process by which candidates register to run for office and meet eligibility requirements. The completed roster sets the stage for campaign season in St. Lucie County ahead of the 2026 elections.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as first St. Lucie County student named Southeast Youth of the Year
cards.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of Port St.
cards.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of Port St. Lucie High School, has made history as the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to be named Southeast Region Youth of the Year. He will compete for the national title at the National Youth of the Year competition on Oct. 1 in New York City. The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award recognizes standout teens across the Boys & Girls Clubs community who demonstrate dedication to academics, strong values, and leadership in service.

Enrique arrived from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without speaking English. Through encouragement from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he transformed from a newcomer in Port St. Lucie to the graduating valedictorian. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, noted that while Enrique's achievement is historic, his character impresses most. This fall, Enrique will attend the University of Florida.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce teen shooting sparks community safety concerns
cards.teaser: The critical shooting of a Fort Pierce teenager has raised concerns among local residents about youth safety in the community.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce teenager remains in critical condition following a shooting that has heightened community concerns about youth violence. Three juveniles have been arrested in connection with the incident, which occurred recently in Fort Pierce.

Local residents have expressed alarm about the shooting. "It's terrifying because it could be your child," one community member said, reflecting fears about youth safety in Fort Pierce neighborhoods.

hero.headline: Multi-vehicle crash closes northbound I-95 lanes near Vero Beach
hero.teaser: A multi-vehicle crash Saturday night shut down multiple lanes on northbound I-95 near Vero Beach.
hero.body:
The crash occurred on Saturday, June 13, blocking multiple northbound lanes of Interstate 95 in the Vero Beach area. Details about the number of vehicles involved and whether anyone was injured were not available in initial reports.

The lane closures affected northbound traffic near Vero Beach. Motorists were advised to expect delays in the area.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with grandmother's murder
cards.teaser: A Vero Beach man was charged with his grandmother's murder following a monthslong investigation.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office charged the man after investigators determined he allegedly cleaned the scene and moved the body. The arrest came after a months-long investigation into the grandmother's death.

The investigation concluded with the filing of murder charges on Saturday, June 13. The suspect remains in custody.

cards.headline: Man accused of cleaning crime scene after Vero Beach grandmother's death
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff's Office alleges a man cleaned the scene and moved his grandmother's body after her death.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the man accused of killing his Vero Beach grandmother allegedly cleaned the crime scene and moved her body. The allegations emerged during the investigation into the grandmother's death.

The sheriff's office announced the charges on Friday, June 12. The case involves evidence that the suspect attempted to conceal the crime by altering the scene where his grandmother died.

cards.headline: Indian River Lagoon residents sought for protection program
cards.teaser: Residents living directly on the Indian River Lagoon are being asked to participate in protecting the waterway.
cards.body:
A program is seeking participation from residents whose properties border the Indian River Lagoon. The initiative aims to involve waterfront property owners in conservation and protection efforts for the lagoon.

The program was announced on Friday, June 12. Property owners with direct access to the Indian River Lagoon can participate in the protection initiative.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie teen named Southeast Youth of the Year
cards.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of St. Lucie High School, became the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to win the regional honor.
cards.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz has made history as the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to be named Southeast Region Youth of the Year. The St. Lucie High School valedictorian will compete for the national title at the National Youth of the Year competition on October 1 in New York City. Enrique arrived from the Dominican Republic eight years ago without speaking English. Through encouragement from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he seized opportunities to grow and thrive, eventually becoming both the county's Youth of the Year and Florida Youth of the Year before heading to the University of Florida in the fall.

Community leaders have praised Enrique's accomplishments and character. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, said Enrique's achievement is historic but that his character impresses most, noting he has turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others with humility and determination. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and longtime Youth of the Year judge, said Enrique stood out from the start and believes he is ready for the national competition. Enrique's parents expressed overwhelming pride in seeing their son reach his goals and credited Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping him grow as a leader and person.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Pride memorial delayed by new state DEI restrictions
cards.teaser: A proposed rainbow pyramid monument honoring Pulse nightclub victims faces obstacles from Senate Bill 1134.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee has designed a rainbow pyramid monument to honor the 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre, which occurred 10 years ago on June 12. The proposed memorial would be illuminated at night and etched with the meaning behind each color. Committee member Ronnie Dunayer believes Old School Square would be the perfect location, situated near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where a Pride mural once stood before being sandblasted away by the Florida Department of Transportation in August 2025.

The memorial's progress faces legal obstacles from Senate Bill 1134, which awaits the governor's decision. The bill, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and could put state funding at risk. Commissioner Juli Casal acknowledged the challenge, stating that private funding and private property could accelerate the process, as the city would not need to be involved. Dunayer said private funding and private property could allow the memorial to be completed "tomorrow."

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The measure would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, potentially reducing county revenue by approximately $50 million by 2028. County Commission Vice Chair Laura Moss said the state-mandated change amounts to a declaration of war on local government. "The state is going to dictate to the local governments how we fund whatever it is we fund. Every county is different," Moss said. "We fund what the community wants." Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called the amendment "an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy," characterizing it as a tax shift rather than a genuine tax cut.

According to the Tax Payers Association, the $50 million loss represents a significant portion of the county's $597 million budget. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of funding coming from ad valorem taxes. The shortfall could prevent construction of three projected fire stations. Lunceford warned the county would need to raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate for lost revenue, potentially increasing costs for government services through impact fees and utility fees.
